prompt.en: A trainee wants to tape a high-voltage cabinet interlock closed for an open-cover test. Which plan preserves the protections taught in this lesson?

text.en: Keep the bypass and rely on the original fuse to prevent a shock.

feedback.en: A fuse protects wiring from overcurrent. A dangerous body current can be far below the fuse rating.

text.en: Keep the interlock functional; use qualified de-energized service, controlled discharge, and meter verification.

feedback.en: Do not defeat the interlock. Removing input power and verifying stored-charge discharge address different hazards.

text.en: Remove the bypass and begin internal work as soon as the cover switch opens.

feedback.en: The interlock may remove input power, but it does not prove capacitors are discharged. Verification is still required.

text.en: Keep the bypass and use a smaller fuse as the main personal shock protection.

feedback.en: A fuse is not a replacement for an enclosure interlock or safe service procedures. Changing its rating does not establish shock safety.

explanation.en: Interlocks, fuses, de-energizing, and stored-energy control serve different safety functions. Preserve each protection rather than substituting one for another.

prompt.en: A test point moves from 1.5 m to 3.0 m from an unchanged antenna. In the simple free-space point-source model, how does power density compare?

text.en: About one quarter of the original value.

feedback.en: Distance doubled. Squaring the distance ratio gives four, so power density becomes a quarter. This is a model, not a site exposure assessment.

text.en: About one half of the original value.

feedback.en: A half corresponds to the field-strength ratio in this model. Power density follows the square of that ratio.

text.en: About the same as the original value.

feedback.en: Fixed transmitter power does not mean fixed density at every distance. The energy spreads over more area.
Moving farther away reduces power density in this model. It does not concentrate the same power into the farther point.

explanation.en: In the stated free-space model, field strength varies with inverse distance and power density with inverse distance squared. Real exposure assessment needs more than this ratio.

prompt.en: An indoor transmitting antenna has low SWR. People can still approach its main beam. Which plan addresses human RF exposure rather than equipment matching?

text.en: Retune for an even lower SWR, keeping people and power unchanged.

feedback.en: A lower SWR improves the equipment match. It does not establish safe exposure for nearby people.

text.en: Raise power to improve the link while keeping people in the same places.

feedback.en: More power can increase exposure. Link strength alone does not establish a safe occupied area.

text.en: Keep power and access unchanged after confirming frequency stability.

feedback.en: Frequency stability is a signal-quality requirement, not a human exposure assessment.

text.en: Reassess distance, beam direction, power, operating time, and access to the antenna.

feedback.en: Exposure depends on the radiated field and where people can be. Use the relevant exposure framework; low SWR is not clearance.

explanation.en: Equipment matching and human exposure are separate checks. Antenna placement, beam direction, power, time, and access all affect the exposure plan.
